# Setup

```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Load the modeling packages, set chunk display options, and fix the random seed for reproducibility.
# Load packages and set a reproducible random seed.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
required_packages <- c("tidyverse", "rpart", "randomForest", "glmnet", "xgboost")
missing_packages <- required_packages[
  !vapply(required_packages, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
]
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Install these packages first: ", paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}
library(tidyverse)
library(rpart)
library(randomForest)
library(glmnet)
library(xgboost)
set.seed(415)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
```

# Load Training, Testing, and Validation Data

```{r load_model_data}
# Locate the project data folder, load the existing train/test/validation splits, and verify required variables.
# Find the repository data directory from the root or code/ folder.
project_root <- if (file.exists("data/split/training_data.csv")) {
  "."
} else if (file.exists("../data/split/training_data.csv")) {
  ".."
} else {
  stop("Cannot find data/split/training_data.csv. Open the project .Rproj first.")
}

# Load the original split datasets without overwriting them.
split_dir <- file.path(project_root, "data", "split")
required_files <- c("training_data.csv", "test_data.csv", "validation_data.csv")
for (filename in required_files) {
  if (!file.exists(file.path(split_dir, filename))) {
    stop("Missing required data file: ", file.path(split_dir, filename))
  }
}
training_data <- read.csv(file.path(split_dir, "training_data.csv"))
testing_data <- read.csv(file.path(split_dir, "test_data.csv"))
validation_data <- read.csv(file.path(split_dir, "validation_data.csv"))

# Check the predictor and outcome columns before modeling.
model_columns <- c("PHQ", "GAD", "gender", "field", "race.2",
                   "yr_sch.2", "fincur.2", "age")
for (dataset_name in c("training_data", "testing_data", "validation_data")) {
  missing_columns <- setdiff(model_columns, names(get(dataset_name)))
  if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
    stop(dataset_name, " is missing: ", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
  }
}

# Confirm the three dataset sizes.
dim(training_data)
dim(testing_data)
dim(validation_data)
```

# Prepare Predictive Modeling Data

```{r model_01_prepare_predictive_modeling_data}
# Keep complete cases for the outcomes and demographic predictors in each data split.
train <- training_data %>%
  select(
    PHQ,
    GAD,
    gender,
    field,
    race.2,
    yr_sch.2,
    fincur.2,
    age
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

test <- testing_data %>%
  select(
    PHQ,
    GAD,
    gender,
    field,
    race.2,
    yr_sch.2,
    fincur.2,
    age
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

validation <- validation_data %>%
  select(
    PHQ,
    GAD,
    gender,
    field,
    race.2,
    yr_sch.2,
    fincur.2,
    age
  ) %>%
  drop_na()
```

# Set Factor Levels

```{r normalize_stem_labels}
# Standardize STEM and non-STEM labels across all three datasets before fitting models.
# Match the STEM labels used in the earlier analysis.
for (dataset_name in c("train", "test", "validation")) {
  dataset <- get(dataset_name)
  dataset$field <- as.character(dataset$field)
  dataset$field[dataset$field == "NotSTEM"] <- "Non-STEM"
  assign(dataset_name, dataset)
}
```


```{r model_02_set_factor_levels}
# Set consistent factor categories and reference levels so predictions use the same coding across datasets.
race_levels <- c("White", "Asian", "Black", "Hispanic", "Middle Eastern")
year_levels <- c("firstyear", "secondyear", "thirdyear", "fourthyear+")

train$gender <- factor(
  train$gender,
  levels = c("Men", "Women")
)

test$gender <- factor(
  test$gender,
  levels = c("Men", "Women")
)

validation$gender <- factor(
  validation$gender,
  levels = c("Men", "Women")
)

train$field <- factor(
  train$field,
  levels = c("Non-STEM", "STEM")
)

test$field <- factor(
  test$field,
  levels = c("Non-STEM", "STEM")
)

validation$field <- factor(
  validation$field,
  levels = c("Non-STEM", "STEM")
)

train$race.2 <- factor(
  train$race.2,
  levels = race_levels
)

test$race.2 <- factor(
  test$race.2,
  levels = race_levels
)

validation$race.2 <- factor(
  validation$race.2,
  levels = race_levels
)

train$yr_sch.2 <- factor(
  train$yr_sch.2,
  levels = year_levels
)

test$yr_sch.2 <- factor(
  test$yr_sch.2,
  levels = year_levels
)

validation$yr_sch.2 <- factor(
  validation$yr_sch.2,
  levels = year_levels
)
```

# Check Dataset Sizes

```{r model_03_check_dataset_sizes}
# Confirm the number of complete observations available for training, testing, and validation.
dim(train)
dim(test)
dim(validation)
```

**Interpretation:** The models are built using the official training dataset. The testing dataset is used to compare the different approaches, while the validation dataset is kept separate to check how the strongest models perform on new observations.

# Depression Prediction Models

## Depression Baseline Model

```{r model_04_depression_baseline_model}
# Predict test-set depression scores using the mean PHQ score in the training data as a baseline.
phq_baseline_value <- mean(
  train$PHQ
)

phq_baseline_pred <- rep(
  phq_baseline_value,
  nrow(test)
)

phq_baseline_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_baseline_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_baseline_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_baseline_pred
  )
)

phq_baseline_r2 <- 0
```

**Interpretation:** The baseline model predicts the same average depression score for every student. It gives us a simple starting point to compare the other models against.

## Depression Linear Regression

```{r model_05_depression_linear_regression}
# Fit a multiple linear regression predicting PHQ from GAD and student characteristics.
phq_lm <- lm(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)

summary(phq_lm)

phq_lm_pred <- predict(
  phq_lm,
  newdata = test
)

phq_lm_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_lm_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_lm_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_lm_pred
  )
)

phq_lm_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_lm_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** The linear regression uses anxiety and the student characteristics together to predict depression. This model performed much better than simply predicting the average depression score for every student.

## Depression Gender x STEM Regression

```{r model_06_depression_gender_x_stem_regression}
# Add a gender-by-STEM interaction to test whether the PHQ prediction relationship varies across groups.
phq_interaction <- lm(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender * field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)

summary(phq_interaction)

phq_interaction_pred <- predict(
  phq_interaction,
  newdata = test
)

phq_interaction_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_interaction_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_interaction_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_interaction_pred
  )
)

phq_interaction_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_interaction_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** This model allows the relationship between gender and depression to depend on whether a student is in STEM. It performed almost exactly the same as the regular linear regression.

## Depression Regression Tree

```{r model_07_depression_regression_tree}
# Fit a regression tree to predict PHQ using anxiety and student characteristics.
phq_tree <- rpart(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train,
  method = "anova"
)

phq_tree_pred <- predict(
  phq_tree,
  newdata = test
)

phq_tree_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_tree_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_tree_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_tree_pred
  )
)

phq_tree_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_tree_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** The regression tree was able to predict depression better than the baseline, but it had more prediction error than the regression-based models.

## Depression Random Forest

```{r model_08_depression_random_forest}
# Train a random forest to predict PHQ and generate test-set predictions.
set.seed(415)

phq_rf <- randomForest(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train,
  ntree = 500
)

phq_rf_pred <- predict(
  phq_rf,
  newdata = test
)

phq_rf_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_rf_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_rf_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_rf_pred
  )
)

phq_rf_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_rf_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** Random Forest predicted depression fairly well, but it did not improve prediction compared with the simpler regression models.

## Prepare Depression Data for Ridge and LASSO

```{r model_09_prepare_depression_data_for_ridge_and_lass}
# Convert depression predictors into numeric design matrices for penalized regression.
phq_x_train <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)[, -1]

phq_x_test <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = test
)[, -1]

phq_x_validation <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = validation
)[, -1]
```

## Depression Ridge Regression

```{r model_10_depression_ridge_regression}
# Use cross-validation to tune a ridge regression model for PHQ prediction.
set.seed(415)

phq_ridge <- cv.glmnet(
  x = phq_x_train,
  y = train$PHQ,
  alpha = 0
)

phq_ridge_pred <- predict(
  phq_ridge,
  newx = phq_x_test,
  s = "lambda.min"
)

phq_ridge_pred <- as.numeric(
  phq_ridge_pred
)

phq_ridge_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_ridge_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_ridge_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_ridge_pred
  )
)

phq_ridge_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_ridge_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** Ridge regression performed well, but its prediction error was slightly higher than the ordinary linear regression.

## Depression LASSO Regression

```{r model_11_depression_lasso_regression}
# Use cross-validation to select the LASSO penalty for PHQ prediction.
set.seed(415)

phq_lasso <- cv.glmnet(
  x = phq_x_train,
  y = train$PHQ,
  alpha = 1
)

phq_lasso_pred <- predict(
  phq_lasso,
  newx = phq_x_test,
  s = "lambda.min"
)

phq_lasso_pred <- as.numeric(
  phq_lasso_pred
)

phq_lasso_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_lasso_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_lasso_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_lasso_pred
  )
)

phq_lasso_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_lasso_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** LASSO was also one of the strongest depression models. Its results were almost identical to the ordinary linear regression and Gender x STEM regression.

## Depression XGBoost

```{r model_12_depression_xgboost}
# Fit an XGBoost model for PHQ and predict depression scores in the test set.
phq_xgb_train <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)[, -1]

phq_xgb_test <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = test
)[, -1]

phq_xgb_validation <- model.matrix(
  PHQ ~ GAD +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = validation
)[, -1]

set.seed(415)

phq_xgb <- xgboost(
  x = phq_xgb_train,
  y = train$PHQ,
  nrounds = 100,
  objective = "reg:squarederror"
)

phq_xgb_pred <- predict(
  phq_xgb,
  phq_xgb_test
)

phq_xgb_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_xgb_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_xgb_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_xgb_pred
  )
)

phq_xgb_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_xgb_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** XGBoost predicted depression fairly well, with a testing RMSE of about 0.471 and an R-squared of about 0.555. However, it did not outperform the simpler regression models.

# Depression Test-Set Comparison

```{r model_13_depression_test_set_comparison}
# Compare depression models on the held-out test data using the performance metrics defined below.
depression_results <- data.frame(

  Model = c(
    "Baseline",
    "Linear Regression",
    "Gender x STEM Regression",
    "Regression Tree",
    "Random Forest",
    "Ridge Regression",
    "LASSO Regression",
    "XGBoost"
  ),

  RMSE = c(
    phq_baseline_rmse,
    phq_lm_rmse,
    phq_interaction_rmse,
    phq_tree_rmse,
    phq_rf_rmse,
    phq_ridge_rmse,
    phq_lasso_rmse,
    phq_xgb_rmse
  ),

  MAE = c(
    phq_baseline_mae,
    phq_lm_mae,
    phq_interaction_mae,
    phq_tree_mae,
    phq_rf_mae,
    phq_ridge_mae,
    phq_lasso_mae,
    phq_xgb_mae
  ),

  R2 = c(
    phq_baseline_r2,
    phq_lm_r2,
    phq_interaction_r2,
    phq_tree_r2,
    phq_rf_r2,
    phq_ridge_r2,
    phq_lasso_r2,
    phq_xgb_r2
  )
)

depression_results <- depression_results[
  order(depression_results$RMSE),
]

depression_results
```

**Interpretation:** The Gender x STEM regression had the lowest depression testing RMSE at 0.4630, but regular linear regression and LASSO were almost identical. Random Forest and XGBoost performed a little worse, so the more complicated machine learning methods did not improve depression prediction.

```{r model_14_depression_test_set_comparison}
# Plot test-set performance across the depression prediction models.
ggplot(
  depression_results,
  aes(
    x = reorder(Model, RMSE),
    y = RMSE
  )
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Depression Model Comparison on Testing Data",
    x = NULL,
    y = "RMSE"
  )
```

**Interpretation:** The regression-based models had the lowest depression prediction error. Random Forest and XGBoost were still much better than the baseline, but they did not beat the simpler regression approaches.

# Anxiety Prediction Models

## Anxiety Baseline Model

```{r model_15_anxiety_baseline_model}
# Predict test-set anxiety scores using the mean training-set GAD score as a baseline.
gad_baseline_value <- mean(
  train$GAD
)

gad_baseline_pred <- rep(
  gad_baseline_value,
  nrow(test)
)

gad_baseline_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$GAD - gad_baseline_pred)^2
  )
)

gad_baseline_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$GAD - gad_baseline_pred
  )
)

gad_baseline_r2 <- 0
```

**Interpretation:** The baseline anxiety model predicts the same average anxiety score for every student and gives us a starting point for comparing the other models.

## Anxiety Linear Regression

```{r model_16_anxiety_linear_regression}
# Fit a multiple linear regression predicting GAD from PHQ and student characteristics.
gad_lm <- lm(
  GAD ~ PHQ +
    gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)

summary(gad_lm)

gad_lm_pred <- predict(
  gad_lm,
  newdata = test
)

gad_lm_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$GAD - gad_lm_pred)^2
  )
)

gad_lm_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$GAD - gad_lm_pred
  )
)

gad_lm_r2 <- cor(
  test$GAD,
  gad_lm_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** The linear regression predicted anxiety much better than the baseline model. Depression was especially useful for predicting anxiety.

## Anxiety Gender x STEM Regression

```{r model_17_anxiety_gender_x_stem_regression}
# Include a gender-by-STEM interaction in the anxiety regression model.
gad_interaction <- lm(

)

  abs(

  )
)

gad_interaction_r2 <- cor(
  test$GAD,
  gad_interaction_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** Adding the Gender x STEM interaction produced almost the same anxiety prediction performance as regular linear regression.

## Anxiety Regression Tree

```{r model_23_anxiety_xgboost}
  )
)

gad_xgb_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$GAD - gad_xgb_pred
  )
)

gad_xgb_r2 <- cor(
  test$GAD,
  gad_xgb_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** XGBoost predicted anxiety fairly well, with a testing RMSE of about 0.552 and an R-squared of about 0.555. However, it did not outperform LASSO or the simpler regression models.

# Student Characteristics Only

These models remove the other mental health score to see how well the student characteristics predict depression and anxiety on their own.

## Depression Using Student Characteristics Only

```{r model_26_depression_using_student_characteristics_o}
# Fit a PHQ regression using only student characteristics, without GAD as a predictor.
phq_student <- lm(
  PHQ ~ gender +
    field +
    race.2 +
    yr_sch.2 +
    fincur.2 +
    age,
  data = train
)

summary(phq_student)

phq_student_pred <- predict(
  phq_student,
  newdata = test
)

phq_student_rmse <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test$PHQ - phq_student_pred)^2
  )
)

phq_student_mae <- mean(
  abs(
    test$PHQ - phq_student_pred
  )
)

phq_student_r2 <- cor(
  test$PHQ,
  phq_student_pred
)^2
```

**Interpretation:** Using only student characteristics, the model explained about 13% of the variation in depression and had an RMSE of about 0.657. This was much weaker than the models that also included anxiety.

# Final Summary

Depression and anxiety were both significantly higher in the post-COVID sample. Depression increased from about 1.89 to 1.99, while anxiety increased from about 1.98 to 2.15. The subgroup results also showed that the increases were present for both men and women and for both STEM and non-STEM students. The interaction models showed that the increases were larger for women and for STEM students.

For prediction, the simpler regression models performed the best overall. For depression, the Gender x STEM regression had the lowest testing RMSE at 0.4630, although regular linear regression and LASSO were almost exactly the same. For anxiety, LASSO had the lowest testing RMSE at about 0.543, again with the Gender x STEM and regular linear regression models extremely close.

Random Forest and XGBoost did not improve prediction compared with the simpler regression approaches. XGBoost had a testing RMSE of about 0.471 for depression and about 0.552 for anxiety. It also had higher prediction error than the strongest regression models on the validation data.

The validation results were very close to the testing results, which shows that the strongest models continued to perform well on new observations. The Gender x STEM regression had the lowest validation RMSE for both depression and anxiety, although its performance was almost identical to linear regression and LASSO.

The other mental health score was the most useful part of prediction. Student characteristics alone explained only about 13% of the variation in depression or anxiety, while including anxiety when predicting depression or depression when predicting anxiety increased R-squared to about 57%. Overall, the results suggest that simpler regression models were enough for these data and that the more complicated machine learning models did not add meaningful predictive improvement.
